CONTENT: A sea-crossing passage in which the water itself is described as legally divided: at an unmarked line on the open sea — one body of water indistinguishable to the eye from the water on either side of it — one sea ends and another begins, one jurisdiction's waters cease and another's commence, the change registered not by anything visible in the sea but by a chart, a logbook entry, a ship's instrument or the recording of a position. The label "Mare duality" suggests the source named the sea twice (two names for the same stretch, perhaps a Latin or old name against a modern one, or territorial versus international water), the duality turning on an act of naming rather than on any alteration in the thing named.

AGENTS: The sea (or a named stretch of it) as the thing that changes name without changing itself; a vessel and those aboard it crossing the line; the external marker that makes the boundary perceptible — a chart, map, log, instrument, treaty or register — and, behind it, the naming or law-making authority that drew the line.

ECHOED_WORDS: "ceases" / "ends" and "begins" / "commences" (the cessation/recommencement predicates); "the same water"; "boundary" or "line"; "invisible"; "chart" / "map" / "the log"; the doubled sea-names; possibly "is called" or "takes the name of".

CONTENT: A passage about a stretch of sea and the legal boundary that divides it — most likely a ship's passage across a line of latitude/longitude or a maritime jurisdictional limit, at which the same unchanging water (or the vessel upon it, or a body of water such as a sea or gulf) ceases to be one named/owned thing and becomes another: territorial sea becoming high sea, one nation's waters becoming another's, one named sea ending and the next beginning. The crossing is imperceptible to the eye — the water looks identical on both sides, no mark, no line, no change in colour or swell — and is registered only by an external instrument or document: a chart, a chronometer, a log-book entry, a ship's papers, a treaty or map. The label here, "mare duality," suggests the passage played on the doctrine of mare liberum versus mare clausum (free sea / closed sea), the same sea being simultaneously free and owned depending on which juridical system names it.

AGENTS: The sea or a particular body of water (the "one and the same thing" that changes name); a ship and those aboard it crossing the line; a navigator or officer who consults the instrument and records the crossing; the chart, log, clock, or treaty as the external marker that alone makes the boundary perceptible; by implication the states or legal systems whose competing nomenclatures meet at the line.

ECHOED_WORDS: "the same water"; "ceases to be" / "begins to be"; "invisible"; "no mark upon the sea"; "mare liberum" / "mare clausum"; the naming of two seas or two jurisdictions; "chart," "log," "chronometer," "instrument," "record," "papers."
